turns.doctor_question: Hello, and welcome. I'm Dr. [Name], a psychiatrist. Thank you for coming in today. What brings you to the clinic?
turns.patient_response:
Hi, Doctor. Well, what brings me in is... I keep getting these flashes. They just hit me completely out of nowhere. It's like I'm right back in that crowded holding room, seeing the fight happen all over again and hearing everybody get shoved up against the wall. 

It's really intense. Like, I'll just be standing at a pickup counter for work, waiting on a package, and suddenly I'm right back in that room. I just need it to stop.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient describes experiencing recurrent, intrusive flashbacks where they feel as though they are suddenly back in a traumatic holding room witnessing a fight.

turns.doctor_question: When did this incident in the holding room happen? How long ago was it?
turns.patient_response: It was about a week ago. I was... well, I was detained overnight, and that's when I saw that assault happen in the holding area. So, yeah, this has all been going on for about a week now, ever since that night.

turns.doctor_question: When you have these flashes and you're back in that holding room, do you feel like you're actually experiencing it happening right now in the present moment, or do you experience it more like you're remembering it and watching it from the outside?
turns.patient_response: Honestly, I'm not really sure. It's... it's confusing. I don't think I'm just watching it from the outside, though. It feels more like I'm actually there, experiencing it right in that moment all over again. I'm just... back in that room, hearing the yelling and the shoving. But then I snap out of it and realize I'm at work. So I don't know exactly what you'd call that, I just know it feels really real when it happens.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient describes dissociative flashback reactions where they feel as though they are actually back in the holding room experiencing the trauma all over again.

turns.doctor_question: During these flashbacks, are you aware that you're actually at work or in your current location, or does it feel like you've completely lost track of where you really are in that moment?
turns.patient_response: I completely lose track of where I am. It's like... the pickup counter or wherever I actually am just disappears. In that moment, I'm just in the holding room. I don't realize I'm at work until it passes and I snap back to reality.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient describes severe dissociative flashback experiences where they completely lose awareness of their present surroundings and feel as though they are back in the traumatic event.

turns.doctor_question: During these flashbacks, do you ever feel like your body doesn't belong to you, or like you're watching yourself from outside your body, or like the world around you seems unreal or dreamlike?
turns.patient_response: No, I don't think so. I mean, I definitely lose track of where I am, like I said, but I don't feel like I'm outside my body or anything like that. And the world doesn't feel like a dream. It just feels... real. Like I'm really back in that room. But I don't feel disconnected from myself, if that makes sense.

symptom_reasoning.S082: The patient explicitly denies experiencing depersonalization or derealization, stating they do not feel outside their body, disconnected from themselves, or that the world feels like a dream.

turns.doctor_question: During these flashbacks when you're back in that holding room, do things around you ever feel foggy, unclear, or like they're happening in slow motion? Or does your sense of time feel strange?
turns.patient_response: No, not really. It doesn't feel foggy or in slow motion or anything like that. When it happens, everything just feels fast and loud, just like it did when it actually happened. Time doesn't feel strange, it just feels like I'm right back in it, exactly how it was.

symptom_reasoning.S069: The patient describes experiencing episodes where they feel as though they are 'right back in it, exactly how it was,' confirming dissociative flashback reactions.
symptom_reasoning.S082: The patient explicitly denies symptoms of derealization or time distortion, stating things do not feel foggy, in slow motion, or strange in terms of time.

turns.doctor_question: Between these flashbacks, when you're not having one, have you noticed that you feel kind of emotionally numb or disconnected from things? Like, do things that normally matter to you feel less important or you just don't feel much of anything?
turns.patient_response: No, I haven't really noticed that. I don't feel numb or disconnected from things. I still care about the stuff that normally matters to me. I mean, I'm just trying to get through the day and finish my deliveries, but... yeah, I wouldn't say I feel empty or like I don't feel anything. I definitely still feel things normally when I'm not having one of those episodes.

symptom_reasoning.S025: The patient denies a loss of interest, stating they still care about the things that normally matter to them.
symptom_reasoning.S076: The patient explicitly denies emotional numbness or emptiness, noting they still feel things normally.

turns.doctor_question: Since this happened a week ago, have you been trying to avoid things that remind you of that night in the holding room? Like, are you staying away from certain places or situations because they might trigger these flashbacks?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, I definitely have. I've actually been turning down all my night runs for work lately. And I've been taking the long way around town on my routes because... well, I just can't make myself go anywhere near that detention building. I also really try to avoid talking about what happened with anyone. If I talk about it, or even get close to that side of town, I just start feeling like I'm right back in there again.

symptom_reasoning.S070: The patient explicitly confirms avoiding work night runs, detouring to avoid the detention building, and avoiding talking about the traumatic event to prevent feeling like they are back there.

turns.doctor_question: Since this happened a week ago, have you noticed that you're more on edge or jumpy than usual? Like, do sudden noises or movements startle you more easily now?
turns.patient_response: Yeah, very much so. I mean, my job has me around noise all day, but now... every time the radio crackles in the van, or I hear a siren, or someone just slams a door, I jump out of my skin. It's like I'm bracing to get rushed all over again. And it's not just a quick flinch, you know? My heart starts pounding so hard after it happens that I actually have to pull the van over or step outside just to catch my breath. I'm just constantly on edge.

symptom_reasoning.S080: The patient explicitly confirms an exaggerated startle response, describing jumping out of their skin and severe, prolonged physiological reactions to everyday sudden noises like sirens, radio crackles, or slammed doors.
